clips.title: Deriving the Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse via SVD
clips.hook: Invert U, Σ, Vᵀ one at a time to get A† = VΣ⁻¹Uᵀ.
clips.summary: With the economy SVD A=UΣVᵀ, invert each factor: Uᵀ for U, Σ⁻¹ for Σ, V for Vᵀ, giving A† = VΣ⁻¹Uᵀ and x̃ = A†b. This is the left pseudoinverse, the closest one can get to inverting a non-square matrix.
clips.videoTitle: Linear Systems of Equations, Least Squares Regression, Pseudoinverse

quiz.question: Given the economy SVD A=UΣVᵀ, what is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse?
options: V Σ⁻¹ Uᵀ
V Σ Uᵀ
U Σ⁻¹ Vᵀ
Uᵀ Σ⁻¹ V
quiz.explanation: Inverting each factor in order gives V Σ⁻¹ Uᵀ, using orthonormality of U and V.

clips.title: Min-Norm and Least-Squares Optimality of A†b
clips.hook: What the pseudoinverse solution means: minimum 2-norm or minimum residual.
clips.summary: In the underdetermined case, x̃=A†b is the solution with minimum 2-norm among all exact solutions. In the overdetermined case it minimizes ‖Ax−b‖₂, the least-squares solution that underlies linear regression.
clips.videoTitle: Linear Systems of Equations, Least Squares Regression, Pseudoinverse

quiz.question: What does x̃=A†b give when A is tall and Ax=b has no exact solution?
options: The x minimizing ‖Ax−b‖₂
The x with minimum ‖x‖ satisfying Ax=b
The x with all residuals zero
The x maximizing ‖Ax‖
quiz.explanation: It is the least-squares solution, minimizing the 2-norm of the residual.

clips.title: Encapsulation: Message, Segment, Datagram, Frame
clips.hook: How each layer wraps the PDU above with its own header, and how headers are stripped on the way up.
clips.summary: Each layer adds its header to the higher-layer PDU: message becomes segment (ports/reliability info), datagram (IP addresses), then frame. Going down headers are added; going up they are read, acted on, and removed.

quiz.question: In encapsulation, what happens to a transport segment at the network layer?
options: It is converted into a frame directly by the transport layer
It is wrapped with a network header (e.g., IP addresses) to form a datagram
It is split into messages
Its header is removed and discarded at the sender
quiz.explanation: The network layer treats the segment as payload and adds header H_n to create a datagram.

clips.title: Semantic Gap: Rich vs Simple ISA Data Types
clips.hook: Why putting hash tables or matrices into the ISA shifts complexity between compiler and hardware.
clips.summary: Higher-level ISA data types shrink the semantic gap between language and ISA, but make instructions and microarchitecture more complex. RISC supports only simple types, while VAX had queues and linked lists. Specialized domains like ML revive the question of whether matrices should be ISA types.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Comp. Arch. - Lecture 10a: Instruction Set Architecture (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

quiz.question: What is the main trade-off of adding high-level data types (e.g. hash table) directly to the ISA?
options: Smaller semantic gap for software but more complex hardware/instructions
No effect on hardware complexity
Simpler hardware and simpler compilers
Larger semantic gap but simpler compilers
quiz.explanation: Rich ISA types reduce the semantic gap, easing the compiler/programmer's job, but the microarchitect must implement complex instructions.

clips.title: PC-Relative Addressing and Its Range Limit
clips.hook: How LD computes its address with the incremented PC plus a sign-extended 9-bit offset, and why reach is limited.
clips.summary: LD computes address = PC+1 + SEXT(offset9), loads through MAR/MDR into the destination. With 9 bits the reach is about ±256 words, so it cannot address the full 16-bit space and only suits nearby data.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Comp. Arch. - Lecture 10a: Instruction Set Architecture (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

quiz.question: Why is LC-3 PC-relative addressing limited in reach?
options: Memory is only 512 words
The PC is only 9 bits wide
Offsets are unsigned
Only a 9-bit signed offset is available, giving about ±256 words from PC+1
quiz.explanation: The encoded offset is 9 bits two's complement, restricting the target to nearby locations.

clips.title: Indirect Addressing (LDI): Double Memory Access
clips.hook: LDI reads a pointer from memory then dereferences it, reaching anywhere in memory.
clips.summary: LDI computes a PC-relative address, reads a 16-bit value from there, uses it as a new address in MAR, and reads memory again. This enables pointer-style access to any location at the cost of two memory accesses and more datapath states.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Comp. Arch. - Lecture 10a: Instruction Set Architecture (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

quiz.question: How many memory accesses does LC-3 LDI perform, and why is it useful?
options: One; it uses base register
Two; the first fetches a pointer that addresses the operand anywhere in memory
Two; both fetch the operand
Zero; it uses registers only
quiz.explanation: First access gets the pointer, second uses it as address, so the operand can be anywhere.

clips.title: LUI + ORI: Building 32-bit Constants in MIPS
clips.hook: Why a 32-bit instruction cannot hold a 32-bit immediate and how MIPS composes one.
clips.summary: LUI puts a 16-bit immediate in the upper half and zeros the lower half; ORI then fills the lower half. Two instructions are needed since opcode and register fields consume instruction bits.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Comp. Arch. - Lecture 10a: Instruction Set Architecture (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

quiz.question: Why does MIPS need two instructions to load an arbitrary 32-bit constant?
options: Registers are 16 bits
The 32-bit instruction must also hold opcode and register fields, leaving only 16 immediate bits
LUI is the only instruction that writes registers
Memory is not word addressable
quiz.explanation: Instruction encoding space limits the immediate to 16 bits.

clips.title: BEQ in MIPS vs Multi-Instruction Compare in LC-3
clips.hook: Compare a powerful compare-and-branch with LC-3's NOT/ADD/BRz sequence.
clips.summary: MIPS beq compares two registers and branches in one instruction; LC-3 needs NOT, ADD, then BRz using condition codes. Simpler ISA means more instructions, while the powerful instruction needs more complex hardware.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Comp. Arch. - Lecture 10a: Instruction Set Architecture (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

quiz.question: How does LC-3 test r0 == r1?
options: Use a BEQ instruction
Compute r0 + (-r1) into a register and branch if Z is set
XOR then branch on N
Compare via the MAR
quiz.explanation: Negate r1 with NOT+ADD 1, add to r0, and the written result sets Z if equal; then BRz.

clips.title: Why nullptr beats NULL: overload resolution
clips.hook: NULL is an integer, so f(NULL) picks f(int) over f(char*). nullptr fixes this.
clips.summary: NULL is defined as 0 or 0L, an integer type, so overload resolution prefers an int overload over a pointer overload. nullptr has its own type that converts to any pointer type but never to an integer type.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: Pointers and Memory - Ben Saks - CppCon 2020

quiz.question: Given overloads f(int) and f(char*), why does f(NULL) typically call f(int)?
options: NULL is defined as an integer constant (0 or 0L), so it matches int better
NULL is a pointer that is implicitly converted to int
NULL has type std::nullptr_t
Overloads are resolved by declaration order
quiz.explanation: NULL expands to an integer-typed zero, so the int overload is the better match. nullptr_t never converts to integers.

clips.title: Pointer arithmetic: addition, subtraction, one-past-end
clips.hook: Pointer addition scales by element size. Subtraction is only defined within one array.
clips.summary: p+k points k elements later, and the compiler scales by sizeof(T). Subtracting pointers gives the index difference, but only for pointers into the same array or to the one-past-the-end position. Otherwise the behavior is undefined.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: Pointers and Memory - Ben Saks - CppCon 2020

quiz.question: When is subtracting two pointers well-defined?
options: Always, if they have the same type
Only when the result is non-negative
Only when both point to heap memory
Only when both point into the same array or one past its end
quiz.explanation: The standard defines pointer subtraction only within a single array object, including the one-past-the-end position.

clips.title: Subscript is pointer arithmetic; array-to-pointer decay
clips.hook: x[i] is defined as *(x+i), and decay is a momentary conversion.
clips.summary: The subscript operator is defined in terms of pointers, so x[i] and *(x+i) generate identical code. An array decays to a pointer to its first element only momentarily, like a temporary conversion of int to double. The array itself stays an array.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: Pointers and Memory - Ben Saks - CppCon 2020

quiz.question: What does array-to-pointer decay in 'p = x;' do to x?
options: Yields a temporary pointer value to x[0] and x remains an array
Copies the whole array into p
Permanently turns x into a pointer
Makes x const
quiz.explanation: Decay produces a pointer value for the expression only, and x keeps its array type.

clips.title: Arrays aren't pointers (except as parameters)
clips.hook: sizeof, assignment and alignof differ for arrays and pointers. Array parameters are pointers.
clips.summary: You can't assign to an array, and sizeof gives the total byte size of an array but the pointer size for a pointer. A parameter declared as an array type is adjusted to a pointer, so sizeof on it yields the pointer size.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: Pointers and Memory - Ben Saks - CppCon 2020

quiz.question: In void f(char x[32]), what is sizeof(x)?
options: sizeof(char*)
It is a compile error
quiz.explanation: An array parameter is adjusted to a pointer, so sizeof gives the pointer size.

clips.title: Signed/unsigned comparison pitfalls with ptrdiff_t
clips.hook: A negative ptrdiff_t compared with a size_t becomes huge, and auto hides it.
clips.summary: When a signed value is compared with an unsigned value of the same size, the signed value is converted to unsigned. A negative value becomes a huge positive one. Using auto can hide which type you have, and C++20 added ssize for this reason.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: Pointers and Memory - Ben Saks - CppCon 2020

quiz.question: What happens when a negative ptrdiff_t is compared with a size_t of the same width?
options: Compared mathematically, so negative is smaller
Compile error
The negative value is converted to unsigned and becomes very large
Undefined behavior
quiz.explanation: The usual arithmetic conversions turn the signed value into unsigned, so a negative value wraps to a huge one.

clips.title: Index Nested Loop Join and Its Link to Hash Join
clips.hook: Replace the inner scan with an index probe, and see how a hash join is just an ad hoc index.
clips.summary: With an index on the inner table, each outer tuple does a probe, so cost is M + m·C where C depends on the index type and data. A hash join is like building a temporary hash index and discarding it, as SQL Server does with temporary indexes.
clips.videoTitle: #12 - Hash Joins, Sort-Merge Joins, Nested Loop Join Algorithms (CMU Intro to Database Systems)

clips.title: Sort-Merge Join Cost and When It Wins
clips.hook: Sort cost plus a single merge pass, and why sorted inputs or ORDER BY favor it.
clips.summary: Cost is the external sort cost of both tables plus M+N for the merge in the best case without backtracking. Backtracking depends on duplicates, so it isn't in the formula. It wins when inputs are already sorted or the output needs ordering on the join key.
clips.videoTitle: #12 - Hash Joins, Sort-Merge Joins, Nested Loop Join Algorithms (CMU Intro to Database Systems)

clips.title: Bloom Filters in Hash Joins
clips.hook: Sideways information passing: a Bloom filter built during the build phase skips useless probes.
clips.summary: While building the hash table, also build a Bloom filter and pass it to the probe side. Probes check the cheap filter first and skip the hash table on misses. This helps most for selective joins, giving up to about 2x speedup.
clips.videoTitle: #12 - Hash Joins, Sort-Merge Joins, Nested Loop Join Algorithms (CMU Intro to Database Systems)

quiz.question: When is a Bloom filter in a hash join most beneficial?
options: When the join is highly selective and most probe tuples have no match
When the build table is huge
When nearly all probe tuples match
When the join is a cross join
quiz.explanation: Misses are rejected cheaply by the filter, avoiding hash table lookups and key comparisons.

clips.title: Recursive Partitioning and Grace Hash Join Cost
clips.hook: Handling skewed partitions with rehashing, and why the cost is 3(M+N).
clips.summary: If a partition does not fit in memory, repartition it with a different hash function or seed, leaving other partitions alone. Degenerate cases with all-equal keys can't be fixed, so fall back to block nested loop. Cost is about 3(M+N): read and write during partitioning, then read during the probe.
clips.videoTitle: #12 - Hash Joins, Sort-Merge Joins, Nested Loop Join Algorithms (CMU Intro to Database Systems)

quiz.question: Why is the Grace hash join estimated at 3(M+N) I/Os?
options: Three hash functions are used
Each table is sorted three times
Three buffer pages are used
Read both tables, write partitions, then read the partitions back
quiz.explanation: Partitioning reads and writes each table (2(M+N)), then the probe phase reads partitions again ((M+N)).

clips.title: Hybrid Hash Join: Keep the Hot Partition in Memory
clips.hook: Keep one partition resident and join it immediately, spilling the rest.
clips.summary: Hybrid hash join keeps a hot partition in memory as a live hash table and joins it during the partitioning pass, spilling only the others to disk. This saves I/O but is hard to get right, since predicting the hot partition is difficult and the memory might be better used otherwise.
clips.videoTitle: #12 - Hash Joins, Sort-Merge Joins, Nested Loop Join Algorithms (CMU Intro to Database Systems)

clips.title: Gradient components as relative importance of weights
clips.hook: Reading the gradient as a sensitivity vector: a gradient of (3,1) means x matters 3x more.
clips.summary: Each gradient component gives the sign of the needed nudge and, via relative magnitude, how sensitive the cost is to that parameter. A gradient of (3,1) means locally that changing x has three times the effect of changing y.
clips.videoTitle: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn | Deep Learning Chapter 2

quiz.question: If the gradient of f at a point is (3,1), what does this imply?
options: Locally, f is three times as sensitive to x as to y
The minimum is at (3,1)
Steps should be taken along (3,1) to decrease f
f equals 3x+y everywhere
quiz.explanation: Partial derivatives measure local sensitivity; the negative gradient, not the gradient, is the descent direction.

clips.title: What the trained network actually learned
clips.hook: Hidden-layer weights look random and the net is confidently wrong on noise.
clips.summary: The ~96% accurate network's first-layer weights do not form edge detectors; it found a local minimum that classifies well without those features. Random noise inputs yield confident outputs because the cost never rewarded calibrated uncertainty.
clips.videoTitle: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn | Deep Learning Chapter 2

quiz.question: Why does the network confidently classify random noise?
options: The cost only trained on clean centered digits and rewarded confidence, never uncertainty on out-of-distribution input
Noise resembles a 5
Gradient descent failed to converge
Sigmoid activations saturate at 0.5
quiz.explanation: The training distribution and cost give no incentive for uncertainty off-distribution.

clips.title: Memorization vs structure in optimization
clips.hook: Networks fit shuffled labels, but learning curves reveal structured data is easier to optimize.
clips.summary: Deep nets can reach full training accuracy on randomly shuffled labels, so low training cost alone doesn't imply learned structure. Training on random labels descends slowly and roughly linearly, while structured data drops quickly, and local minima found are of similar quality.
clips.videoTitle: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn | Deep Learning Chapter 2

quiz.question: What does fitting randomly shuffled labels to 100% training accuracy show?
options: Gradient descent cannot work on noisy labels
Test accuracy will match training accuracy
The network generalizes well
Large networks can memorize data, so minimizing training cost doesn't guarantee learned structure
quiz.explanation: High capacity allows memorization; generalization requires structure in the data.

clips.title: Immutable URLs + long max-age: versioned asset caching
clips.hook: Why versioned filenames let you cache for a year without ever revalidating.
clips.summary: If a URL's content never changes, you can set max-age to a year, and browsers/CDNs will serve it without contacting the server. Updates ship under new URLs (script-v2.js), so the HTML references the new version and stale entries are simply evicted by the cache over time.
clips.videoTitle: Browser Caching Best Practices,  When to use no-cache vs max-age without breaking your site

quiz.question: With versioned immutable assets (script-v1.js, cats-v1.jpg) and max-age of one year, a new page references script-v2.js, styles-v2.css and cats-v1.jpg. What happens?
options: Only v2 JS and CSS are fetched from the server; cats-v1.jpg is served from cache without contacting the server
All three files are refetched because the page HTML changed
cats-v1.jpg is revalidated with If-None-Match
The cache purges all v1 files immediately
quiz.explanation: Cache keys are URLs; cats-v1.jpg is still fresh, so it's reused without network. Only unseen URLs miss.

clips.title: no-cache vs no-store vs must-revalidate, with 304s
clips.hook: no-cache doesn't mean 'don't cache': it means store but revalidate every time.
clips.summary: no-cache lets the cache store the response but requires revalidation before each reuse using Last-Modified/If-Modified-Since or ETag/If-None-Match. An unchanged resource gets a tiny 304 Not Modified, while a changed one returns a full response. no-store forbids storage, and must-revalidate only applies after max-age expires.
clips.videoTitle: Browser Caching Best Practices,  When to use no-cache vs max-age without breaking your site

quiz.question: What does Cache-Control: no-cache require of a cache holding a stored copy?
options: It may reuse the copy for max-age seconds
It must not store the response at all
It must refetch the full body every time
It must revalidate with the origin before each reuse, possibly receiving a 304
quiz.explanation: no-cache permits storage but forces validation before reuse; a 304 avoids resending the body. no-store is the one that prevents storage.

clips.title: Why max-age on mutable, interdependent assets breaks pages
clips.hook: Partial cache eviction plus max-age can mix old and new files and corrupt your page.
clips.summary: With max-age on mutable URLs, a cache may evict one of several dependent resources (e.g. the CSS) early. The refetch then returns the new version while the others stay old, so the page ends up with mismatched versions. A hard refresh bypasses max-age and masks the bug, making the site seem flaky.
clips.videoTitle: Browser Caching Best Practices,  When to use no-cache vs max-age without breaking your site

quiz.question: Why can max-age=600 on mutable script.js, styles.css and the HTML yield a broken page even within the 10 minutes?
options: The server's clock drifts from the client's
ETags are invalid within max-age
Browsers ignore max-age for CSS
The browser may evict only some entries, so a refetched file is the new version while the others are stale
quiz.explanation: Caches may evict at any time. A refetched resource is current, while the still-cached ones are old, so the page mixes versions.

clips.subtopic: how a CPU works datapath and control
clips.title: Instruction Bits Driving Load/Store Control Signals
clips.hook: See how opcode bits and decoders generate register and memory enable signals for load and store.
clips.summary: Instruction bits feed decoders. The opcode decoder outputs gate the register decoder's read and write enables, so a load enables the memory read and register write, and a store does the reverse. For non-register instructions, no enable reaches the registers, so their values are kept safe.
clips.videoTitle: CRAFTING A CPU TO RUN PROGRAMS

quiz.question: In this design, why are the opcode decoder's outputs combined with the register-select decoder's outputs?
options: To increase the width of the data bus
To ensure only one of a register's read or write enable fires, depending on instruction type, and none for other instructions
To compute the ALU result faster
To increment the address register
quiz.explanation: The register-select decoder alone would assert both read and write enables. Gating with the instruction-type decoder selects one and suppresses both for other instructions.

clips.subtopic: how a CPU works datapath and control
clips.title: Why x86 Binaries Don't Run on ARM
clips.hook: Different wiring of instruction register outputs gives the same bits different meanings.
clips.summary: Two circuits that differ only in how the instruction register outputs are wired interpret identical bit patterns differently, as a store in one and a load in the other. This is why a binary built for one architecture is meaningless on another.
clips.videoTitle: CRAFTING A CPU TO RUN PROGRAMS

clips.subtopic: how a CPU works datapath and control
clips.title: ALU Datapath: Multiplexers, Operand Select and Result Register
clips.hook: How arithmetic instructions route two register operands through muxes into the ALU and back.
clips.summary: Arithmetic instructions need two registers read at once, so each register's own data line goes to two multiplexers, one per ALU input. The instruction fields select the operands and the ALU opcode. The result is held in a temporary register because the destination register, which is also the first operand, can't be written while it is being read.
clips.videoTitle: CRAFTING A CPU TO RUN PROGRAMS

quiz.question: Why is the ALU result stored in a temporary register before being written to the destination register?
options: The destination is also the first operand being read, so it can't be written at the same time
Registers cannot store ALU output directly
The ALU is too slow to drive the registers
The multiplexers need to be reset by the OS
quiz.explanation: The destination register is also an operand source being read. The result is latched temporarily so the control unit can reconfigure the signals for the write.

clips.subtopic: single cycle and multi cycle processors
clips.title: Dataflow Execution Model: Firing on Operand Readiness
clips.hook: No program counter: instructions fire when operands arrive, with results routed by destination pointers.
clips.summary: In dataflow, ordering comes only from data dependences. Each node names its destination(s) and fires when all operand tokens arrive, so many instructions can fire concurrently. This contrasts with the von Neumann control-flow order set by the PC.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Circuits - Lecture 13: Multi-Cycle Microarchitecture (ETH Zurich, Spring 2017)

quiz.question: In a pure dataflow machine, what determines when an instruction executes?
options: The order of instructions in memory
A compiler-assigned cycle number
Availability of all its operand tokens
The program counter reaching its address
quiz.explanation: Instructions fire when all input operands are available; ordering is only by data dependences, enabling parallelism.

clips.subtopic: single cycle and multi cycle processors
clips.title: Dataflow Nodes: Token Matching and ISA Encoding
clips.hook: How a dataflow node knows its operands are ready: destination pointers, presence bits and matching logic.
clips.summary: A dataflow instruction encodes its operation, sources and destinations. A producer sends its result to the destination's memory location and sets the presence bit for the correct operand slot. Matching logic fires the node when both bits are set. Fan-out needs multiple destinations or a copy node.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Circuits - Lecture 13: Multi-Cycle Microarchitecture (ETH Zurich, Spring 2017)

quiz.question: How does a dataflow node typically detect that both operands have arrived?
options: The ALU stalls until memory returns
It polls the program counter
A matching logic checks presence bits set by producers for each operand slot
A global clock counter tells it when to fire
quiz.explanation: Producers write the result into the consumer's slot and set that operand's bit; matching logic fires when all are set.

clips.subtopic: single cycle and multi cycle processors
clips.title: ISA Contract vs Microarchitecture: Hidden Reordering
clips.hook: ISA promises a sequential model; hardware may run dataflow-style internally if results look sequential.
clips.summary: Control-driven vs data-driven execution can be chosen separately at ISA and microarchitecture levels. Out-of-order machines expose sequential von Neumann semantics but reorder internally, reporting results in program order.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Circuits - Lecture 13: Multi-Cycle Microarchitecture (ETH Zurich, Spring 2017)

quiz.question: Why can an out-of-order processor execute instructions in dataflow order yet remain correct?
options: It forbids dependent instructions
It makes results visible to software in the order the ISA specifies
It changes the ISA semantics
It uses no registers
quiz.explanation: The microarchitecture must honor the ISA contract when making results architecturally visible.

clips.subtopic: single cycle and multi cycle processors
clips.title: Three Microarchitecture Design Principles
clips.hook: Critical path, common-case (Amdahl) and balanced design, and how single-cycle violates them.
clips.summary: Reduce the critical path by splitting long paths across cycles, optimize the common case per Amdahl's law, and balance work across stages and components (e.g., fetch width matching decode width). Single-cycle gives little freedom for any of them.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Circuits - Lecture 13: Multi-Cycle Microarchitecture (ETH Zurich, Spring 2017)

clips.subtopic: single cycle and multi cycle processors
clips.title: Multi-Cycle as an FSM: States Defined by Control Signals
clips.hook: Instruction processing as an FSM with shared fetch/decode and per-instruction subgraphs.
clips.summary: Instruction processing is an FSM; a state is defined by asserted control signals, which govern the data path and next-state control generation. Fetch/decode are shared, then instruction-specific subgraphs return to fetch. Generating control early avoids lengthening the critical path.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Circuits - Lecture 13: Multi-Cycle Microarchitecture (ETH Zurich, Spring 2017)

clips.subtopic: single cycle and multi cycle processors
clips.title: Building a Multi-Cycle MIPS Datapath for lw
clips.hook: Step through lw: add IR and per-stage registers, reuse one memory and the ALU, PC+4 through ALU.
clips.summary: Starting from single-cycle, the design uses one memory and the ALU for everything. lw is split into fetch (into instruction register), register read, sign-extended address calculation, memory read, and write back, with registers latching intermediates. PC increment reuses the ALU.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Circuits - Lecture 13: Multi-Cycle Microarchitecture (ETH Zurich, Spring 2017)

quiz.question: In the multi-cycle MIPS design, how is PC+4 computed without a dedicated adder?
options: A second memory computes it
It is skipped
The shared ALU adds 4 to the PC with muxed inputs during fetch
The register file adds it
quiz.explanation: Muxes select PC and constant 4 as ALU inputs, and the result is written to the PC.

clips.subtopic: single cycle and multi cycle processors
clips.title: Multi-Cycle MIPS Controller FSM
clips.hook: Fetch, decode, address gen, mem read, writeback: the main FSM with states shared across instructions.
clips.summary: Fetch asserts signals and increments PC, decode asserts none, and opcode selects branches: memory address generation shared by lw/sw, then memory read and write-back, or execute then ALU writeback for R-type, or the branch state. Each state transition determines control signals for the next cycle.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Circuits - Lecture 13: Multi-Cycle Microarchitecture (ETH Zurich, Spring 2017)

clips.title: Why Stack Access Is Just a Stack-Pointer Add
clips.hook: See in assembly why a local needs no allocation call but a heap object does.
clips.summary: A stack variable's address is a compile-time constant offset from the stack pointer (e.g. rsp+12 passed in rdi), so locating it costs one add and the compiler can often eliminate it entirely. A heap object requires calling operator new, receiving an address at runtime, and passing it via a pointer, which is why heap access means indirection and is slower.
clips.videoTitle: C++ Weekly - Ep 496 - Stack vs Heap

quiz.question: Why is obtaining the address of a local variable cheaper than that of a heap-allocated object, per the compiler output shown?
options: The address is a fixed offset from the stack pointer known at compile time, while heap address comes from a runtime call to operator new
Stack variables live in registers permanently
Stack variables are never passed by reference
The heap is always swapped to disk
quiz.explanation: Locals are at rsp+constant, computed with one add (or eliminated). Heap addresses are only known after operator new returns.

clips.title: Value category belongs to expressions, not objects
clips.hook: A named T&& variable has rvalue-reference type but is an lvalue expression.
clips.summary: Value category is a property of an expression, not of an object. A named rvalue reference parameter has type T&& but, because it has a name and address, the expression is an lvalue, so it can't be passed to a T&& parameter without std::move.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: Master C++ Value Categories With Standard Tools - Inbal Levi - CppCon 2022

quiz.question: Given Data&& a = Data{}; why does foo(a) fail where foo takes Data&&?
options: a is a const object
Rvalue references cannot be copied
foo must be a template
a is an lvalue expression despite its rvalue reference type
quiz.explanation: Id-expressions naming a variable are lvalues regardless of the declared type.

clips.title: Reference binding rules by value category
clips.hook: Which value categories bind to which reference types, and the lifetime extension rules.
clips.summary: Rvalues bind to const T&, T&& and const T&&; lvalues bind only to T& and const T&. Const lvalue refs and rvalue refs extend temporary lifetime, which explains why const rvalues pick the copy constructor.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: Master C++ Value Categories With Standard Tools - Inbal Levi - CppCon 2022

quiz.question: Which overloads can bind a const prvalue (result of a function returning const Data)?
options: T& only
T&& only
T& and T&&
const T& and const T&&
quiz.explanation: const prvalue cannot bind to non-const refs; it binds to const T& and const T&&, with const T&& preferred when present.

clips.title: Guaranteed copy elision and prvalue materialization
clips.hook: C++17 makes prvalues initializers rather than temporaries, materialized only when needed.
clips.summary: Since C++17 copy/move elision for prvalue initialization is mandatory, so Data d = Data{42} constructs once. A prvalue is converted to an xvalue via temporary materialization, which requires a complete type.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: Master C++ Value Categories With Standard Tools - Inbal Levi - CppCon 2022

quiz.question: In C++17, Data d = Data(42); calls which constructors?
options: Constructor then move
Constructor then copy
Only the constructor
Implementation defined
quiz.explanation: Guaranteed elision initializes d directly from the prvalue.

clips.title: Reference collapsing and forwarding references
clips.hook: How && in a template deduces to T& for lvalues and why it isn't just an rvalue ref.
clips.summary: When references combine via typedefs or templates, they collapse: only two rvalue references give an rvalue reference. In a deduced template T&& parameter, lvalues deduce T as U&, collapsing to U&, preserving the argument's value category.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: Master C++ Value Categories With Standard Tools - Inbal Levi - CppCon 2022

quiz.question: With template<class T> void f(T&&), calling f(x) for an lvalue int x deduces the parameter type as:
options: int
int&
int&&
const int&&
quiz.explanation: T deduces to int&, and int& && collapses to int&.

clips.subtopic: functional dependencies and normal forms BCNF
clips.title: Super Keys vs Candidate Keys
clips.hook: Define super keys and candidate keys through functional determination and minimality.
clips.summary: A super key is any attribute set that functionally determines all attributes of the relation. A candidate key is a minimal super key, meaning removing any attribute breaks this. A relation can have several candidate keys, and the primary key is one chosen candidate key.

quiz.question: Which statement about keys is correct?
options: Every super key is a candidate key
A candidate key is a minimal super key, and a relation can have several
The set of all attributes is never a super key
A relation has exactly one candidate key
quiz.explanation: Candidate keys are minimal super keys, and multiple minimal ones can exist. The full attribute set is always a super key.

clips.title: ISA as a Contract: State-Machine View
clips.hook: Microarchitecture can be arbitrarily fancy as long as architectural state transitions obey the ISA.
clips.summary: The processor is modeled as a state machine where architectural state (e.g., register contents) moves from S0 to S1 per instruction. Any microarchitectural technique is legal provided the resulting state respects the ISA specification, which is the contract enabling performance and security innovation underneath.

quiz.question: What constraint does the ISA place on microarchitectural optimizations?
options: The architectural state after each instruction must match what the ISA specifies
They must use the same cache sizes
They must not change instruction latency
They must use the same pipeline depth
quiz.explanation: Only the architectural state seen by the programmer is constrained; timing and structures are free.

clips.title: RISC vs CISC and x86's Micro-op Decoder
clips.hook: Where to place the ISA abstraction: semantic gap, instruction count, and x86 cracking CISC into micro-ops.
clips.summary: CISC puts the ISA close to high-level languages with complex multi-cycle instructions, while RISC keeps simple instructions and a larger semantic gap. Instruction count depends on both compiler and ISA; x86 is CISC externally but decodes into RISC-like micro-ops using a decoder costing about 2% of chip area.

quiz.question: How does modern x86 reconcile its CISC ISA with RISC-style execution?
options: The compiler emits only simple instructions
A decoder translates CISC instructions into micro-operations
Complex instructions run in software emulation
The ISA is changed per generation
quiz.explanation: Intel decodes x86 instructions into micro-ops executed by a RISC-like core.

clips.title: Deriving Bayes' Theorem: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior
clips.hook: Generalize the counting argument into the formula and see why the sample size cancels.
clips.summary: The posterior P(H|E) equals P(H)P(E|H) divided by P(H)P(E|H)+P(¬H)P(E|¬H). The arbitrary population size cancels, and the denominator is P(E) expanded via total probability over H and ¬H.
clips.videoTitle: Bayes theorem, the geometry of changing beliefs

quiz.question: In Bayes' theorem, why is the denominator typically computed as P(H)P(E|H)+P(¬H)P(E|¬H)?
options: Because H and E are independent
Because P(E) is rarely known directly, so it is expanded by total probability over H and ¬H
Because likelihoods must sum to 1
To normalize the prior to 1
quiz.explanation: P(E) is the total probability of the evidence, found by summing over the disjoint cases where H is true and false.

clips.title: The Area Diagram for Bayes' Theorem
clips.hook: Use a unit square to rederive Bayes and see why irrelevant evidence changes nothing.
clips.summary: Treat possibilities as a unit square with the hypothesis as a strip of width P(H). Evidence shrinks each side by its likelihood, and the posterior is the hypothesis's share of the restricted region. Equal likelihoods leave the proportion unchanged, so irrelevant evidence does not update belief.
clips.videoTitle: Bayes theorem, the geometry of changing beliefs

quiz.question: In the area diagram, what happens to the posterior if P(E|H)=P(E|¬H)?
options: It becomes P(E)
It equals the prior
It rises to 1
It falls to 0
quiz.explanation: Both regions shrink by the same factor, so the proportion occupied by H is unchanged.

clips.title: Micro-ops: how modern x86 is RISC inside
clips.hook: Why Pentium Pro-era x86 decodes into RISC-like micro-ops, and what that costs in power.
clips.summary: Since the Pentium Pro, Intel decodes complex variable-length x86 instructions into micro-ops, which are RISC-like, and runs those down the pipeline. The cost is a large front-end decoder that uses extra transistors, heat and power, a key reason x86 was less efficient in smartphones.
clips.videoTitle: RISC vs CISC - Is it Still a Thing?

quiz.question: Why does x86 pay a power penalty relative to ARM despite using RISC-like micro-ops internally?
options: Micro-ops execute more slowly than ARM instructions
x86 cannot use branch prediction
x86 has no pipeline
It needs complex front-end logic to decode variable-length instructions into micro-ops
quiz.explanation: The decode and cracking stage for variable-length CISC instructions costs transistors and power that a fixed-length ISA avoids.

clips.title: Aligned Accesses: addr mod size = 0 and Why It's Faster
clips.hook: Why a misaligned access can cost two memory accesses, and how MIPS and x86 treat it differently.
clips.summary: An access of s bytes is aligned if address mod s = 0. A misaligned access can span two words or blocks and need two memory accesses instead of one. MIPS faults on unaligned accesses, x86 permits them, and the compiler generates the addresses.

quiz.question: Why can a 4-byte load from address 7 be slower than one from address 8?
options: Address 7 requires the little-endian alignment network
Registers can only be loaded from even addresses
Address 7 is odd, so it must go through the TLB
The access straddles a word boundary and needs two memory accesses
quiz.explanation: Bytes 7–10 span two aligned words, so two accesses are needed. Address 8 is aligned and needs one.

clips.title: Encoding Key Constraints via Primary Key Choice
clips.hook: Why the primary key of a relationship table shrinks to one entity's key under a key constraint.
clips.summary: For many-to-many, the relationship table's key is the concatenation of participating entity keys. With a key constraint (at most one), the primary key becomes only the key of the constrained side (DID), so each department appears in at most one row.
clips.videoTitle: Lecture 16 Part 14 Converting ER to Relational

quiz.question: In Manages(SSN, DID, since) where each department has at most one manager, which primary key encodes this constraint?
options: DID only
(SSN, DID)
since
SSN only
quiz.explanation: Making DID the primary key makes each DID unique in the table, so a department can be associated with at most one SSN.

clips.title: Collapsing Entity and Relationship Tables
clips.hook: Merge Departments and Manages into one table when DID is the key of both.
clips.summary: With a key constraint, the relationship can be merged into the constrained entity's table (Dept_Mgr) keyed by DID, carrying the relationship attributes and a foreign key to Employees. This avoids a separate table and a join, and works because DID keys both.
clips.videoTitle: Lecture 16 Part 14 Converting ER to Relational

quiz.question: Why can Manages be merged into the Departments table?
options: Because Manages has no attributes
Because Employees has no key
Because DID is a key of both Departments and the Manages relationship
Because relationships must always be merged
quiz.explanation: Each department has at most one manages row, so its attributes and the manager's SSN foreign key fit in one row keyed by DID.

clips.title: Participation Constraints: NOT NULL and ON DELETE NO ACTION
clips.hook: Mapping total participation to SQL DDL, and why it fails for ternary relationships.
clips.summary: Key plus total participation maps to a merged table with PRIMARY KEY(DID) and SSN NOT NULL as a foreign key. ON DELETE NO ACTION blocks deleting a manager who still manages a department. This works for binary relationships; ternary ones need CHECK constraints or similar.
clips.videoTitle: Lecture 16 Part 14 Converting ER to Relational

quiz.question: In Dept_Mgr(DID PRIMARY KEY, SSN NOT NULL REFERENCES Employees ON DELETE NO ACTION), what does ON DELETE NO ACTION do?
options: Deletes the department when the manager is deleted
Allows deletion and leaves a dangling reference
Sets SSN to NULL when the employee is deleted
Aborts deletion of an employee who still manages a department
quiz.explanation: The delete is rejected, which preserves the total participation guarantee that every department has a manager. SET NULL would also violate NOT NULL.

clips.title: L3 End-to-End vs L2 Hop-by-Hop: Router Forwarding
clips.hook: How the router strips the L2 header, does a routing lookup and decides it needs ARP.
clips.summary: The L3 header carries source and destination IPs end to end, while the L2 header is rewritten at each hop. The router strips the incoming frame, looks up the destination in the routing table, finds a directly connected egress interface, and needs an ARP entry for host D.
clips.videoTitle: Packet Traveling - How Packets Move Through a Network

quiz.question: What happens to the L2 header when a router forwards a packet?
options: It is stripped and a new one built for the next hop
It is kept unchanged end to end
Only the source MAC is changed
The L3 header is replaced instead
quiz.explanation: L2 headers are hop-scoped; the router removes the ingress one and builds a new one with its egress MAC and next-hop MAC.

clips.title: High Clock Rate Doesn't Mean High Performance
clips.hook: A 2 GHz CPI-2 chip equals a 1 GHz CPI-1 chip: why frequency alone misleads.
clips.summary: A 2 GHz processor with CPI 2 and a 1 GHz processor with CPI 1 both take 1 ns per instruction. Architects must consider CPI and frequency together, holding instruction count and ISA fixed.

quiz.question: Processor A: 3 GHz, CPI 2.0. Processor B: 2 GHz, CPI 1.2. Same binary. Which is faster?
options: B, about 1.1x faster
A, due to higher frequency
They are equal
A, about 1.1x faster
quiz.explanation: A: 2/3 ≈ 0.667 ns/instr. B: 1.2/2 = 0.6 ns/instr. B is ~1.11x faster.

clips.title: Cross Product and Select: Building Joins by Hand
clips.hook: Cartesian product schema/cardinality, attribute disambiguation, and composing σ and π to express a join query.
clips.summary: The cross product's schema is the union of the two schemas (with name-clash prefixing like Student.SID) and its cardinality is S×A. Combined with a selection enforcing equality on the key and a projection, it expresses a meaningful join query.

quiz.question: Student has 4 attributes and S tuples; Apply has 4 attributes and A tuples. What is the shape of Student × Apply?
options: 7 attributes, S×A tuples
8 attributes, S+A tuples
4 attributes, S×A tuples
8 attributes, S×A tuples
quiz.explanation: Schemas are concatenated (SID is kept twice, qualified by relation name) and every tuple pair appears.

clips.title: Deriving Amdahl's Law from serial/parallel fractions
clips.hook: Derive speedup = 1/(s + f/P) and see why the serial fraction caps performance at 1/s.
clips.summary: Split execution time into a serial fraction s and a perfectly parallelizable fraction f=1-s. Time on P cores is s+f/P, so speedup = 1/((1-f)+f/P), bounded by 1/s as P grows (10% serial gives at most 10x, 1% gives 100x).

quiz.question: A program has 5% serial execution time and the rest is perfectly parallelizable. What is the upper bound on speedup as the number of cores goes to infinity?
quiz.explanation: Speedup is limited to 1/s = 1/0.05 = 20.

clips.title: Amdahl speedup curves and fixed-problem-size assumption
clips.hook: Why the parallel fraction matters more than core count, and what Amdahl's Law silently assumes.
clips.summary: On a log core-count axis, curves for 50%, 75%, 90% and 95% parallel fractions saturate quickly. Even with 16,000+ cores, 95% parallel gives under 20x. Amdahl assumes fixed problem size, unlike Gustafson's law, where runtime stays constant as problems scale.

quiz.question: Which implicit assumption of Amdahl's Law does Gustafson's Law relax?
options: Serial fraction is zero
Communication has no cost
Cores have different speeds
Problem size stays fixed as cores increase
quiz.explanation: Amdahl assumes fixed problem size. Gustafson assumes larger problems keep runtime constant as cores grow.

clips.title: Eigenvectors as vectors that stay on their span
clips.hook: Which vectors does a linear map only scale, and why does that reveal a rotation's axis?
clips.summary: Eigenvectors are nonzero vectors that remain on their own span under a transformation, scaled by the eigenvalue (which may be negative). For the matrix with columns (3,0),(1,2), the eigenvectors are the x-axis (λ=3) and the line through (-1,1) (λ=2). In 3D, a rotation's eigenvector with λ=1 is its axis.
clips.videoTitle: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues | Chapter 14, Essence of linear algebra

quiz.question: Why must the eigenvalue of the eigenvector giving a 3D rotation's axis equal 1?
options: The axis vector is rotated by 360 degrees
Rotation matrices have determinant zero
Eigenvalues of orthogonal matrices are always positive reals
Rotations preserve length, so the axis vector is neither stretched nor squished
quiz.explanation: The axis vector stays on its span, so Av=λv. Rotations preserve length, so |λ|=1, and since the axis is fixed (not flipped), λ=1.

clips.title: Worked cases: rotation, shear, and scaling
clips.hook: Complex roots, repeated roots, and a full eigenspace: what the characteristic polynomial reveals.
clips.summary: For the matrix (3,0),(1,2) the polynomial (3−λ)(2−λ) gives λ=2,3, and solving (A−2I)v=0 gives the span of (-1,1). A 90° rotation gives λ²+1, with only complex roots and so no real eigenvectors. A shear gives (1−λ)², with a single eigenvalue 1 whose eigenvectors form only a line, while uniform scaling by 2 gives a whole plane of eigenvectors.
clips.videoTitle: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues | Chapter 14, Essence of linear algebra

quiz.question: A shear with matrix columns (1,0),(1,1) has characteristic polynomial (1−λ)². What is true of its eigenvectors?
options: There are no real eigenvectors
Every vector in the plane is an eigenvector
Only vectors on the x-axis are eigenvectors, with λ=1
There are two independent eigenvectors with λ=1
quiz.explanation: λ=1 is a repeated root but (A−I) has a one-dimensional kernel, so the eigenspace is only the x-axis. This is why a shear has no eigenbasis.

clips.title: Eigenbasis, diagonalization, and matrix powers
clips.hook: Why changing to an eigenbasis makes A^100 trivial.
clips.summary: If the eigenvectors span the space, changing basis to them turns the transformation into a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues (P⁻¹AP). Powers then reduce to powering the diagonal entries, so compute D^100 and convert back. A shear cannot do this because it lacks enough eigenvectors.
clips.videoTitle: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues | Chapter 14, Essence of linear algebra

quiz.question: How is A^100 computed efficiently when A has an eigenbasis?
options: Raise each entry of A to the 100th power
Multiply A by itself 100 times in the standard basis
Compute P D^100 P⁻¹, where D is diagonal and P holds the eigenvectors
Use only the largest eigenvalue
quiz.explanation: A = P D P⁻¹ gives A^n = P D^n P⁻¹, and D^n just raises each diagonal eigenvalue to the nth power.

clips.title: Set Difference and the Join-Back Trick
clips.hook: Find students who applied nowhere, and recover their names via a join-back after the difference.
clips.summary: Difference of projected ID sets gives students with no applications. Because difference needs matching schemas, to get names you take the ID result and natural join it back with Student, then project name.

quiz.question: Why can't we just project (sID, sName) from Student and subtract the projection of sID from Apply to get names of non-applicants?
options: Difference is not defined on projected relations
Projection removes duplicates so names are lost
Difference only works on single-attribute relations
Difference requires union-compatible schemas, and Apply has no sName
quiz.explanation: Both operands must have the same schema; so compute the ID difference first, then natural join back with Student and project sName.

clips.title: Intersection Is Redundant: Two Derivations
clips.hook: Show E1 ∩ E2 = E1 − (E1 − E2) and also equals E1 ⋈ E2 for equal schemas.
clips.summary: Intersection can be written as E1 − (E1 − E2), shown via Venn diagram. With identical schemas, natural join matches all columns, so it also equals intersection. Hence intersection adds no expressive power.

quiz.question: When E1 and E2 have identical schemas, why does E1 ⋈ E2 equal E1 ∩ E2?
options: Natural join computes a cross product then unions
Natural join requires disjoint schemas
Natural join equates all attributes, keeping only tuples in both
Natural join keeps tuples in E1 only
quiz.explanation: Natural join requires equality on all shared attributes; with the same schema that means the tuple appears in both relations.

clips.title: Why Inheritance Couples Child to Parent's Structure
clips.hook: How a DrawableImage forces bogus load()/save() and why fixing the hierarchy is a costly refactor.
clips.summary: A subclass inherits the parent's entire contract, so DrawableImage is forced to implement load/save and can only throw. Fixing it by inserting FileImage breaks every client expecting Image to have those methods, since bundling commonality into a parent makes each exception require a hierarchy change.

quiz.question: Why is introducing an intermediate FileImage class a costly fix for DrawableImage's unwanted load()/save()?
options: Image can no longer implement resize and flip
The compiler refuses multiple levels of inheritance
Clients that expect Image to expose load/save break, and the hierarchy must be edited
Virtual dispatch becomes impossible for the remaining subclasses
quiz.explanation: Moving load/save out of Image changes the base contract, breaking all code relying on Image having them and forcing edits across the hierarchy.

clips.title: Refactoring to Composition: Decoupled Image Components
clips.hook: Replace subclassing with standalone format classes operating on an Image passed in explicitly.
clips.summary: Image becomes a plain in-memory class, and format classes become standalone with save/load taking an Image rather than using this. Adding ImageDraw requires no changes to existing classes, and apps combine pieces freely per use case.

quiz.question: What makes adding ImageDraw cheap in the composed design?
options: Templates generate the glue code
It inherits from all format classes
Image is not forced to carry shared file-related members, so ImageDraw just takes an Image
It overrides Image's virtual methods
quiz.explanation: No common parent bundles file operations, so a new class simply uses Image without touching others.

clips.title: Interfaces: Abstraction Without Inheriting Implementation
clips.hook: Inheritance gives code reuse plus abstraction; interfaces keep only the contract, enabling dependency injection.
clips.summary: Inheritance bundles reuse with abstraction via the parent's method contract. With composition you recover the abstraction through a minimal interface like ImageFile, easily added to existing classes, and can inject the implementation into the app class (dependency injection).

quiz.question: Why are minimal interfaces easier to evolve than parent classes?
options: They permit private inheritance
They define only the critical contract rather than sharing all state and methods by default
They avoid virtual calls
They are resolved at compile time
quiz.explanation: Parent classes share everything by default, widening coupling; interfaces expose only the contract and can be attached to existing classes.

clips.title: Trade-offs and Safe Inheritance Design
clips.hook: Composition's boilerplate cost versus inheritance, and rules for designing a class to be inherited.
clips.summary: Composition costs boilerplate initialization and forwarding wrappers but shrinks the surface area between objects. If you inherit, avoid protected data, expose an explicit protected override API, and make everything else private or final.

quiz.question: Which guideline makes inheritance safer when changing a parent class?
options: Avoid virtual methods and use only public data
Provide an explicit override API and make everything else private/final
Expose protected data directly
Make all members protected
quiz.explanation: Limiting what subclasses can touch prevents parent changes from breaking unknown child dependencies.

clips.title: SQL Joins Need Explicit Conditions; Bag Semantics and DISTINCT
clips.hook: Why SQL returns duplicates and how explicit join conditions differ from natural join.
clips.summary: SQL requires the join condition to be written explicitly (unlike relational algebra's natural join). SQL uses a multiset model, so projections can yield duplicates, and DISTINCT removes them.

quiz.question: Why does projecting student name and major from student JOIN apply in SQL yield duplicate rows, unlike in relational algebra?
options: SQL is based on a multiset model, so projection does not eliminate duplicates unless DISTINCT is used
SQL joins are always cross products
The join condition is evaluated twice
Duplicates arise only when keys are missing in student
quiz.explanation: SQL relations are bags; projection keeps duplicate tuples (e.g., a student applying to the same major at two colleges) unless DISTINCT is specified.

clips.title: Ambiguous Column Names in Multi-Table SELECT
clips.hook: Why an attribute shared by two tables must be qualified even if the join equates them.
clips.summary: When both relations in FROM have an attribute with the same name, an unqualified reference in SELECT is ambiguous and errors, even if the join condition equates them. You must qualify it with the table name.

quiz.question: In SELECT cname FROM college, apply WHERE college.cname = apply.cname, why is there an error?
options: The unqualified cname is ambiguous since both tables have it, regardless of the equality condition
cname is not a key
DISTINCT is required
Equality of attributes is not allowed in WHERE
quiz.explanation: Name resolution is syntactic: the column reference must identify a single table's attribute, even if values are equal by the predicate.

clips.title: SQL Result Ordering and ORDER BY
clips.hook: SQL results are unordered unless you ask; multi-key ORDER BY with ASC/DESC.
clips.summary: SQL's model is unordered, so the same query may return different row orders at different times. ORDER BY sorts by multiple attributes, with ASC default and DESC per-key, with later keys breaking ties.

quiz.question: For ORDER BY gpa DESC, enrollment, how are rows ordered?
options: GPA descending, ties broken by enrollment ascending
Enrollment first, then GPA
Both descending
Unspecified order within same GPA
quiz.explanation: Keys are applied left to right; ASC is default per key, so DESC applies only to gpa.

clips.title: Pipelining: Latency Rises, Throughput Improves
clips.hook: Why a 20-minute worst-case stage gives 100-minute latency but one completion every 20 minutes.
clips.summary: With stages padded to the worst-case stage time (20 min, 5 stages), single-item latency rises from 60 to 100 minutes. After the pipeline fills, one item completes every 20 minutes, giving 3 per hour.

quiz.question: A 5-stage pipeline has every stage padded to the slowest stage time of 20 min. What are the latency of one item and the steady-state throughput?
options: 20 min latency, 3 per hour
60 min latency, 3 per hour
100 min latency, 3 per hour
100 min latency, 5 per hour
quiz.explanation: Latency = 5 x 20 = 100 min. After the pipeline fills, one item finishes every 20 min, which is 3 per hour.

clips.title: CPI and Cycle Time: Single-cycle vs Multi-cycle vs Pipeline
clips.hook: How pipelining gets a short cycle time and CPI near 1, and why latency doesn't improve.
clips.summary: Single-cycle has CPI 1 but a long cycle (8 ns). Multi-cycle has a short cycle (2 ns) but CPI above 1 (about 4). Pipelining keeps the 2 ns cycle and gets CPI near 1 in steady state, so it improves throughput, not per-instruction latency.

quiz.question: Why does a pipelined CPU achieve CPI ≈ 1 with a short cycle time, unlike a multi-cycle CPU?
options: It uses a longer clock period
It removes the need for multiple stages
It shortens each instruction's total latency
Instructions overlap, so one completes per cycle after the pipeline fills
quiz.explanation: Overlapping stages lets one instruction finish each cycle in steady state. The cycle stays short and per-instruction latency does not shrink.

clips.title: Reuse Without Overriding: Composition Beats Inheritance
clips.hook: Why calling base.Method1() from unrelated subclasses is a misuse of inheritance.
clips.summary: If subclasses only call an inherited method and never override anything, there is no subtype polymorphism, so inheritance is unjustified. Move the shared method into a separate class and have both classes hold or use an instance of it (has-a), which avoids a needless common ancestor.
clips.videoTitle: Only Use Inheritance If You Want Both of These

quiz.question: Two classes each call an inherited Method1() from a common base, and neither overrides anything. What is the best design according to the argument?
options: Make the base class abstract
Extract Method1 into a separate class and have both classes use an instance of it
Keep inheritance but make Method1 virtual
Use multiple inheritance from two bases
quiz.explanation: Only code reuse is needed with no overriding or polymorphic use, so has-a composition is appropriate.

clips.title: Polymorphism Only: Prefer an Interface
clips.hook: If overrides never use inherited state or code, a base class is the wrong tool.
clips.summary: When subclasses override a method without using anything inherited, only subtype polymorphism is needed, so a pure interface suffices. Interfaces are more flexible because a type can implement several of them but typically inherit from only one class.
clips.videoTitle: Only Use Inheritance If You Want Both of These

quiz.question: Why is an interface preferred over a base class when only subtype polymorphism is needed?
options: Interfaces allow shared implementation code
Interfaces are always faster to dispatch
A type can implement multiple interfaces but usually extends only one class
Base classes cannot have virtual methods
quiz.explanation: Interfaces avoid the single-inheritance constraint and do not impose unneeded implementation coupling.

clips.title: Why a WHERE tautology on GPA misses NULL rows
clips.hook: gpa>3.5 OR gpa<=3.5 isn't always true once NULLs exist; IS NULL fixes it.
clips.summary: Comparisons with NULL are neither true nor false, so rows with NULL GPA fail both gpa>3.5 and gpa<=3.5, and a seemingly tautological predicate drops them. Adding OR gpa IS NULL makes the predicate truly exhaustive.

quiz.question: Table has rows with NULL gpa. What does SELECT * WHERE gpa>3.5 OR gpa<=3.5 return for those rows?
options: Query raises an error
They are excluded, since each comparison evaluates to unknown
They are included, since the predicate is a tautology
They are included only if DISTINCT is used
quiz.explanation: NULL compared with anything yields unknown; unknown OR unknown is unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows evaluating to true.

clips.title: Three-valued logic: OR with unknown in WHERE
clips.hook: See how a true disjunct rescues a row whose other operand is unknown.
clips.summary: With gpa>3.5 OR sizeHS<1600, a NULL GPA gives unknown, but a true second disjunct makes the OR true, so the row qualifies. WHERE uses true/false/unknown logic and keeps only true.

quiz.question: For a row with gpa NULL and sizeHS=1500, what is the result of (gpa>3.5 OR sizeHS<1600)?
options: Error
False
True, row included
Unknown, row excluded
quiz.explanation: unknown OR true = true, so the row passes.

clips.title: COUNT DISTINCT ignores NULL but SELECT DISTINCT keeps it
clips.hook: Why count(distinct gpa) gives 7 but select distinct gpa returns 8 rows.
clips.summary: Aggregates like COUNT(attr) skip NULLs, so COUNT(DISTINCT gpa) is 7 even with NULL GPAs. But SELECT DISTINCT gpa returns NULL as its own value, giving 8 rows, an inconsistency to watch for.

quiz.question: GPA column has 7 distinct non-null values and some NULLs. What do count(distinct gpa) and the row count of select distinct gpa give?
options: 7 and 7
8 and 8
7 and 8
8 and 7
quiz.explanation: COUNT ignores NULL, while DISTINCT projection treats NULL as a value group.

clips.title: What Each MIPS Pipeline Stage Does
clips.hook: Walk through IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB and why every instruction visits every stage.
clips.summary: IF fetches and increments PC by 4. ID decodes and reads RS/RT early, possible because MIPS keeps them at fixed fields. EX does ALU ops, effective address (base+imm) or branch condition/target; MEM accesses memory, and WB writes the register file. Instructions with nothing to do in a stage still pass through it to keep the pipeline synchronous.

quiz.question: Why can the register file be read in ID before the instruction is fully decoded in MIPS?
options: Source register specifiers are at fixed positions (RS, RT) in the instruction format
MIPS has only one source register per instruction
The register file is read in the EX stage anyway
Decode is done by the ALU
quiz.explanation: Fixed RS/RT fields allow speculative register reads in parallel with decoding.

clips.title: Pipelining Raises Throughput, Not Latency
clips.hook: How overlapping five stages gives ideal CPI of 1 and why real speedup falls short of 5.
clips.summary: Pipelining does not speed up a single instruction but overlaps instructions so that, once full, one completes per cycle. Ideal speedup equals the number of stages, but is reduced by unbalanced stage delays and stalls from hazards.

quiz.question: Which are reasons the real speedup of a 5-stage pipeline is below 5?
options: Fewer registers
Memory is not used
Unbalanced stage work and pipeline stalls
Instructions are longer
quiz.explanation: The clock must fit the slowest stage, and hazards cause stalls.

clips.title: How the vtable and vptr implement virtual functions
clips.hook: Per-class vtables of function pointers and a hidden per-object vptr drive dynamic dispatch.
clips.summary: If a class has any virtual function, the compiler creates a per-class table of function pointers and adds a hidden vptr to each object. A virtual call looks up the function through the object's vptr, so a derived class's table points to its overrides.
clips.videoTitle: Classes part 18 - Understanding the vtable (Popular interview question) | Modern Cpp Series Ep. 54

quiz.question: In the typical implementation, where is the information that selects the overriding function stored, and what does each object hold?
options: The compiler resolves the call at compile time using the pointer's static type
Each object holds a copy of all virtual function bodies
Each object holds a hash map from function name to address
Each object holds a hidden vptr to its class's shared vtable of function pointers
quiz.explanation: Virtual functions are dispatched through a per-class vtable; each object stores only a vptr to it.

clips.title: INSERT ... SELECT: Building Tuples from a Query
clips.hook: Turn a SELECT into rows for INSERT, with constants and NULL filling the schema.
clips.summary: A SELECT that yields the target table's schema can feed INSERT. Constants and NULL are projected to fill columns, and the query is developed and tested as a SELECT first.

quiz.question: In INSERT INTO Apply SELECT sID, 'CMU', 'CS', NULL FROM Student WHERE sID NOT IN (SELECT sID FROM Apply), what do the constants and NULL do?
options: They create a new table
They are projected as columns so the result matches Apply's schema
They filter the rows of Student
They cause a type error because constants are not allowed in SELECT
quiz.explanation: The SELECT list can include literals and NULL, producing tuples with the target schema for insertion.

clips.title: DELETE with Subqueries Over the Same Table
clips.hook: Delete using a GROUP BY/HAVING subquery, and why some DBMSs reject self-referencing deletes.
clips.summary: DELETE conditions can contain subqueries, for example SID IN a GROUP BY/HAVING query. Some systems, such as MySQL, disallow a subquery that reads the table being deleted from. The workaround is to materialize the subquery into a temporary table first.

quiz.question: Why delete from Apply using a temp table in some systems?
options: Temp tables are faster for every delete
DELETE cannot use IN
Some DBMSs forbid a subquery that reads the table being modified
GROUP BY is not allowed in DELETE
quiz.explanation: Some systems disallow referencing the target table in the subquery, so the ids are materialized separately.

clips.title: UPDATE Driven by Nested Subqueries
clips.hook: Convert a triple-nested SELECT into an UPDATE that targets the max-GPA EE applicants.
clips.summary: The WHERE of an UPDATE can use nested subqueries, which can be tested as a SELECT first. The nested query finds EE applicants whose GPA is at least that of every EE applicant, that is, the maximum.

clips.title: Subqueries in the SET Clause
clips.hook: The right side of SET can be a scalar subquery, and omitting WHERE touches every tuple.
clips.summary: The right-hand side of SET may be a scalar subquery such as MAX(GPA). With no WHERE, every tuple is updated.

clips.title: Pure ALOHA: ACK timeout and random backoff
clips.hook: How pure ALOHA recovers from collisions using ACK timeouts and randomized backoff.
clips.summary: A station transmits whenever it has data and waits for an ACK. If the ACK does not arrive in time, it waits a random backoff time before retransmitting. A fixed wait would make the same stations collide again, so randomization is needed.

quiz.question: Why does pure ALOHA use a random backoff time rather than a fixed one after a missing ACK?
options: A fixed wait would violate the ACK timeout
Random backoff removes the need for acknowledgements
A random wait increases the frame size
Stations that collided would retransmit at the same instant again and collide repeatedly
quiz.explanation: Colliding stations with identical fixed waits would retransmit simultaneously and collide again. Random waits desynchronize them.

clips.title: Vulnerable time of pure ALOHA is 2·Tfr
clips.hook: Why a frame needs a collision-free window of two frame times to succeed.
clips.summary: A frame sent at time t collides with any frame that starts in (t−Tfr, t+Tfr). Overlap of even a single bit, whether the first bit of one frame with the last bit of another, destroys both frames. The vulnerable period is therefore 2·Tfr.

quiz.question: In pure ALOHA with frame time Tfr, a frame starts at time t. Which other frame starts cause a collision with it?
options: Starts in (t−2Tfr, t)
Starts exactly at t only
Starts in (t, t+Tfr) only
Starts in (t−Tfr, t+Tfr)
quiz.explanation: A frame starting up to Tfr earlier overlaps our start, and one starting up to Tfr later overlaps our end. That gives a vulnerable time of 2·Tfr.

clips.title: Pipeline Latches: Why PC+4 Differs Per Stage
clips.hook: Each inter-stage latch holds a different instruction's state; PC+4 in one latch isn't the same as the next.
clips.summary: The decode stage reads the registers, generates control signals, and latches PC+4, the register data and the control bits. Each latch holds state belonging to a different instruction, so the PC+4 in the IF/ID latch is not the PC+4 in the ID/EX latch.

quiz.question: At the end of cycle 2, the IF/ID latch and the ID/EX latch each hold a PC+4 value. How do they relate?
options: They are the same value, copied forward
They belong to different instructions: ID/EX holds the older instruction's PC+4 and IF/ID holds the newer one's
Both are overwritten by the branch target
ID/EX holds PC+4 for the next instruction to be fetched
quiz.explanation: Each latch holds the state of the instruction that just finished the stage before it. The older instruction is one stage ahead of the newer one.

clips.title: Execute Stage: ALU, Branch Target and Shrinking Control Bits
clips.hook: See what the EX/MEM latch stores and why the control bits shrink as an instruction moves down the pipeline.
clips.summary: The execute stage computes the ALU result and the branch target (PC+4+offset). It also evaluates the branch condition. The control signals are consumed stage by stage, so the ID/EX latch holds control bits for EX, MEM and WB, while the EX/MEM latch holds only MEM and WB bits.

quiz.question: Why does the EX/MEM latch carry fewer control bits than the ID/EX latch?
options: Branches don't need control signals
Control signals are recomputed in each stage
The latch has less storage
The EX-stage control bits have already been used, so only the MEM and WB bits still need to travel
quiz.explanation: Control signals travel with the instruction and are consumed stage by stage. Earlier stages' bits are dropped once used.

clips.title: Why the Destination Register Number Travels Down the Pipeline
clips.hook: Writeback occurs 4 cycles after decode, so the rd field must be carried through every latch.
clips.summary: At writeback, the ALU result or loaded data is written to the register file through a path back to stage 2. By then up to five different instructions are in flight, so the destination register number has to be carried in every pipeline latch. Otherwise the result is written to the wrong register, because the instruction currently in decode has a different rd.

quiz.question: Why must rd be propagated through the MEM/WB and earlier latches rather than read from the instruction currently in decode?
options: By write-back, the decode stage holds a different, younger instruction with a different rd
rd changes the ALU operation
It reduces power
The register file has no address input
quiz.explanation: Write-back for instruction 1 happens while instruction 5 is in decode, so using the current instruction's rd would write to the wrong register.

clips.title: Per-Stage Control Signals and Latches Written Every Cycle
clips.hook: How control moves from a single-cycle CPU to a pipeline, and why latches need no write-enable.
clips.summary: In a single-cycle CPU, all control signals are active in the same cycle. In a pipeline, the signals are generated in decode and carried in the latches, so each stage uses its own bits. The pipeline registers are written on every clock edge, so they need no extra write-enable control.

quiz.question: In a basic 5-stage pipeline, why do the pipeline registers need no separate write-enable control signal?
options: They are combinational
They are written only on branches
They are written every clock edge, since every stage advances every cycle
Control is stored in memory
quiz.explanation: With no stalls in the ideal pipeline, each latch captures new data on every clock edge.

clips.title: Why typename Is Needed for Dependent Names
clips.hook: Two-phase lookup: how the compiler parses T::iterator without knowing T.
clips.summary: During phase 1 of template compilation the compiler must know which names are types to parse C++, but a dependent name like vector<T>::iterator cannot be classified until T is known. Writing typename promises it is a type, and instantiation fails if it is not. Whether a name is dependent is decided by T, not by the container.

quiz.question: Why must you write typename before std::vector<T>::iterator inside a template?
options: Because iterator is always a private alias
Because vector is a template class and needs a keyword
Because the name depends on T, so in phase 1 the compiler cannot tell whether ::iterator is a type or a member/value
Because typename forces the name to be resolved at runtime
quiz.explanation: The name is dependent on T. Until instantiation the compiler cannot tell whether it names a type, so typename promises that it does.

clips.title: Virtual Functions, override, and Early vs Late Binding
clips.hook: How a base-class pointer reaches the derived method, and what happens without virtual.
clips.summary: Non-virtual calls are early bound: the static type of the pointer or reference selects the function at compile time, and a same-signature method in the derived class only shadows the base one. With virtual, dispatch is late bound on the dynamic type. The override keyword makes the compiler reject signature mismatches that would otherwise be silently ignored.

quiz.question: Fruit* p = new Orange; p->pieWorthy(); pieWorthy is NOT virtual in Fruit. Which version runs?
options: Undefined behavior
Orange's, because the object is an Orange
Fruit's, because binding uses the static pointer type at compile time
Compile error
quiz.explanation: Without virtual, the call is early bound on the static type Fruit*, so Fruit::pieWorthy runs and Orange's version only shadows it.

clips.title: Why PCA needs scaled variables
clips.hook: See how unit choice alone flips PC1 loadings from 0.99/0.1 to 0.77/0.77.
clips.summary: PCA maximizes variance, so a variable on a 10x larger scale dominates PC1 (0.99 math vs 0.1 reading). Dividing each variable by its standard deviation equalizes scales and removes this bias.

quiz.question: Math scores range 0-100 and reading scores 0-10. PCA on centered, unscaled data gives PC1 loading ≈ 0.99 math, 0.1 reading. Why?
options: Centering removes reading variance
PCA maximizes variance, which depends on measurement scale, so the larger-scale variable dominates
Math is truly 10x more predictive of aptitude
SVD is biased toward the first column
quiz.explanation: PC1 maximizes projected variance; larger-scale variables contribute more variance. Standardizing by std removes the artifact.

clips.title: WHERE vs HAVING: filtering rows vs groups
clips.hook: Why aggregates can't appear in WHERE and how HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY.
clips.summary: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and so cannot use aggregate functions, while HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, so conditions like COUNT(ID) >= 2 go there. Example: grouping employees by city and keeping only groups with count >= 2 leaves Bangalore (3) and Chennai (2).
clips.videoTitle: GROUP BY and HAVING Clause in SQL

quiz.question: Given SELECT City, COUNT(ID) FROM employee GROUP BY City, which is the correct way to keep only cities with at least 2 employees?
options: Add HAVING COUNT(ID) >= 2 after GROUP BY
Add WHERE City >= 2
Use ORDER BY COUNT(ID) >= 2
Add WHERE COUNT(ID) >= 2 before GROUP BY
quiz.explanation: Aggregates are computed per group after grouping, so the predicate on them must be in HAVING. WHERE runs on rows before grouping and cannot reference aggregates.

clips.title: Slotted Aloha: Why Slots Halve the Vulnerable Time
clips.hook: How synchronized slots shrink vulnerable time from 2T to T and remove partial-overlap collisions.
clips.summary: Slotted Aloha divides time into slots and permits transmission only at slot starts. Frames either collide completely in the same slot or not at all, so the vulnerable time is T instead of 2T as in pure Aloha.

quiz.question: Why is the vulnerable time of slotted Aloha one frame time rather than two?
options: Frames start only at slot boundaries, so collisions happen only between frames in the same slot
Stations sense the carrier before sending
Frames are shorter in slotted Aloha
Collided frames are retransmitted immediately
quiz.explanation: Because transmissions are aligned to slot starts, partial overlaps with the start or end of other frames cannot occur. Only frames in the same slot collide, giving a vulnerable period of T.

clips.title: Structural Hazard: Single-Port Memory in a 5-Stage Pipeline
clips.hook: See how a unified single-port memory forces a stall between IF and MEM.
clips.summary: With one single-ported memory, a load's MEM stage in cycle 4 collides with instruction 4's fetch in the same cycle. The hardware cannot serve both, so instruction 4 is delayed one cycle.

quiz.question: In a 5-stage pipeline with a single-ported unified memory, which instruction's fetch conflicts with a load's MEM stage?
options: The next instruction (i+1)
The instruction three after the load (i+3)
The instruction just before the load
The instruction two after the load (i+2)
quiz.explanation: The load is in MEM in cycle 4, when the instruction fetched is the fourth instruction (three after the load), so the fetch must be delayed.

clips.title: RAW Data Hazards and Register-File Timing
clips.hook: Why add→sub→and→or on r1 breaks: the half-cycle register file write/read rule.
clips.concept: RAW hazard and register file timing
clips.summary: The register file is written in the first half of a cycle and read in the second half, so a read in the same cycle as the write sees the new value. Consequently, for an add writing r1 in WB (cycle 5), the sub and and read stale values in ID, while the or reads the correct one. Stalling two cycles would fix it but is too slow.

quiz.question: Assuming register writes occur in the first half of the cycle and reads in the second, which of the instructions following 'add r1,...' (sub, and, or, in order) read a stale r1 without forwarding?
options: All three
sub and and
Only or
Only sub
quiz.explanation: The add writes r1 in cycle 5. sub reads in cycle 3 and and in cycle 4 (stale), while or reads in cycle 5, after the first-half write.

clips.title: Forwarding (Bypassing) to Resolve Data Hazards
clips.hook: Feed ALU results straight from pipeline registers instead of waiting for write-back.
clips.summary: Results exist in the EX/MEM register after cycle 3 and in MEM/WB after cycle 4, so they can be routed to the ALU input when needed in cycles 4 and 5. The third dependent instruction gets the value from the register file, so no stall is needed.

quiz.question: For add r1 followed by sub using r1, from which pipeline register is the value forwarded to the ALU?
options: ID/EX
MEM/WB
The register file
EX/MEM
quiz.explanation: The add's result is in EX/MEM at the start of the sub's EX stage, so it is forwarded from there.

clips.title: Forwarding Unit Hardware: Muxes and Register Comparison
