clips.hook: What the forwarding unit compares and how it steers the ALU input muxes.
clips.summary: The ALU input muxes are widened to select among the register-file value, EX/MEM result, or MEM/WB result. The forwarding unit compares the destination registers in EX/MEM and MEM/WB with the source registers of the instruction in EX, and steers the muxes on a match.

quiz.question: What does the forwarding unit compare to decide on forwarding?
options: Destination registers in EX/MEM and MEM/WB against source registers of the instruction in EX
Opcodes of consecutive instructions
The PC against branch targets
Source registers in IF against destination registers in WB only
quiz.explanation: A match between an older instruction's destination and the EX instruction's source triggers the mux selection.

clips.title: Public, Protected, Private Inheritance Semantics
clips.hook: How inheritance access specifiers rewrite the access of inherited members, plus final.
clips.summary: The inheritance specifier caps the access of inherited public/protected members: public preserves them, protected makes public members protected, private makes all accessible members private. Private parent members stay inaccessible regardless, and final prevents further derivation.

quiz.question: class Fruit has public isSeedless and protected isRound. class Pineapple : private Fruit. What is the access of these members inside a class deriving from Pineapple?
options: Both private in Fruit, so accessible only to Pineapple's friends
Both protected
Both inaccessible
Public and protected respectively
quiz.explanation: Under private inheritance both members become private members of Pineapple, so classes derived from Pineapple cannot access them.

clips.title: Multiple Inheritance and Default Inheritance Access
clips.hook: Forgetting 'public' on a base silently gives private inheritance for classes.
clips.summary: In multiple inheritance each parent needs its own access specifier. If omitted, a class defaults to private inheritance while a struct defaults to public, so omission can silently change the design.

quiz.question: class Luke : public Anakin, Padme {}; What kind of inheritance is used for Padme?
options: Compile error
Private
Public
Protected
quiz.explanation: Specifiers apply per base; for a class the default is private.

clips.title: Composition vs Inheritance for Container APIs
clips.hook: Why wrapping std::vector beats inheriting from it: API control, conversions, and stability.
clips.summary: Inheritance exposes the full parent API and risks undesired implicit conversions, and modifying inherited methods is tricky. Composition requires explicit wrappers but insulates your API from upstream changes and gives complete control.

quiz.question: Which is a key advantage of composition over public inheritance when wrapping an external container class?
options: Smaller object size
The wrapper's API is insulated from changes in the wrapped class
Automatic access to protected members
Faster virtual dispatch
quiz.explanation: Only explicitly written wrappers are exposed, so upstream API changes do not alter yours, and there are no implicit derived-to-base conversions.

clips.title: Nested Classes: Access Rules and Iterators
clips.hook: Why iterators are nested classes and which direction access flows.
clips.summary: A nested class can access all members of the outer class, but not vice versa, hence the friend declaration. Nesting inside a class template gives access to template parameters, simplifying iterator definitions.

quiz.question: Which statement about nested classes is correct?
options: A nested class needs its own template parameters inside a template
The nested class can access the outer class's private members
Nested classes cannot be private
The outer class can access private members of the nested class automatically
quiz.explanation: Nested classes are members and have member access; the reverse needs friend.

clips.title: Diamond Problem and Virtual Inheritance
clips.hook: Ambiguity of duplicated base subobjects and how virtual inheritance yields one copy.
clips.summary: With non-virtual multiple inheritance, MeyerLemon contains two Fruit subobjects, making is_sweet ambiguous. Qualifying works but is questionable. Virtual inheritance in Lemon and MandarinOrange yields a single shared Fruit, at the cost of odd constructor and assignment semantics.

quiz.question: What does making Lemon and MandarinOrange inherit virtually from Fruit change for MeyerLemon?
options: It has one shared Fruit subobject, removing ambiguity
Fruit's members become private
Fruit becomes abstract
Two Fruit copies remain but are auto-merged
quiz.explanation: Virtual bases are shared in the most derived object, so only one Fruit subobject and one is_sweet exist.

clips.title: Convexity of logistic regression cost and gradient descent
clips.hook: Why convex J(w,b) makes initialization nearly irrelevant for gradient descent.
clips.summary: Logistic regression's cost J(w,b) is convex, a single bowl with no spurious local optima, which is a key reason this cost is chosen. Hence gradient descent from any initialization (commonly zero) steps in the steepest-descent direction and reaches the same global minimum.

quiz.question: Why can logistic regression be initialized to zeros while deep nets generally cannot be initialized this way?
options: The convex cost has a single global basin, so the start point does not change where gradient descent converges
Logistic regression has no bias term
Zero initialization is always optimal for any model
Gradient is always zero at the optimum so initialization does not matter
quiz.explanation: Convexity means no bad local optima, so any initialization leads to roughly the same global minimum.

clips.title: The gradient descent update rule and why the sign works
clips.hook: Derive why w := w − α·dJ/dw moves downhill from either side of the minimum.
clips.summary: The update w := w − α dJ/dw uses the slope at the current point. A positive slope decreases w and a negative slope increases w, so both sides move toward the minimum, with α (learning rate) controlling step size.

quiz.question: At a point where dJ/dw < 0, what does the update w := w − α dJ/dw do?
options: Increases w
Decreases w
Sets w to zero
Leaves w unchanged
quiz.explanation: Subtracting α times a negative number adds a positive amount to w, moving right toward the minimum.

clips.title: HAVING vs WHERE: filtering on aggregates
clips.hook: Why aggregates can't appear in WHERE but can in HAVING, which runs after GROUP BY.
clips.summary: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY using aggregate predicates, e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Aggregates in WHERE are errors because WHERE is evaluated per row before groups exist.
clips.videoTitle: Advanced Aggregate Functions in SQL (GROUP BY, HAVING vs. WHERE)

quiz.question: Why does `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1` fail in a GROUP BY query while `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` works?
options: WHERE is evaluated per row before grouping, when aggregates do not yet exist
COUNT is not allowed in SELECT with WHERE
HAVING is faster than WHERE for aggregates
WHERE can only be used on indexed columns
quiz.explanation: Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT. Aggregates are computed after grouping, so only HAVING can filter on them.

clips.title: CSMA: Listen Before Talk and Residual Collisions
clips.hook: Why sensing the carrier still can't eliminate collisions: propagation delay and vulnerable time.
clips.summary: CSMA senses the shared medium before transmitting to reduce collisions. Collisions still occur because a station may sense idle only because another station's first bit hasn't yet arrived, worsening with larger propagation delay.

quiz.question: Why can collisions still occur in CSMA even though every station senses the channel before transmitting?
options: Stations ignore the sensing result with some probability
The channel is always busy in shared media
Frames are too large to sense
Propagation delay means a station may see the channel idle while another's first bit is still in transit
quiz.explanation: Because of finite propagation delay, another station's signal hasn't reached the sensing station yet, so it wrongly sees idle and transmits.

clips.title: 1-Persistent CSMA and Its Delay Sensitivity
clips.hook: Continuous sensing, transmit with probability 1, and why high propagation delay hurts it.
clips.summary: A 1-persistent station continuously senses a busy channel and transmits immediately with probability 1 once it is idle. Multiple waiting stations will therefore collide, and long propagation delay further degrades performance.

quiz.question: In 1-persistent CSMA, what happens when two stations are both waiting for a busy channel to become idle?
options: Both transmit immediately upon idle and collide
Only the one with the earlier frame transmits
They back off randomly and avoid collision
They transmit with probability 1/2
quiz.explanation: Both transmit with probability 1 as soon as the channel is idle, causing a collision.

clips.title: Non-Persistent CSMA: Random Backoff Trade-off
clips.hook: Why not sensing continuously improves utilization but increases delay.
clips.summary: A non-persistent station that finds the channel busy waits a random time before sensing again instead of sensing continuously. This reduces collisions between waiting stations and improves utilization, but the channel may sit idle after a transmission ends, increasing delay.

quiz.question: Compared with 1-persistent CSMA, non-persistent CSMA typically gives:
options: Higher utilization, shorter delay
Same utilization, longer delay
Higher utilization, longer delay
Lower utilization, shorter delay
quiz.explanation: Random waiting avoids synchronized collisions (better utilization) but the channel may idle unnoticed, adding delay.

clips.title: p-Persistent CSMA and Comparing the Three Methods
clips.hook: Slotted channels, transmit with probability p, defer with q=1-p, versus continuous and random sensing.
clips.summary: In slotted channels, a p-persistent station with an idle channel transmits with probability p and defers to the next slot with probability q=1-p, repeating until it transmits or another station begins. The comparison shows 1-persistent reacts instantly to idle, non-persistent samples at random times, and p-persistent senses continuously but randomizes its transmission.

quiz.question: In p-persistent CSMA, when a station finds the channel idle at the start of a slot, it:
options: Waits a random time then senses again
Transmits only with probability 1-p
Always transmits
Transmits with probability p, defers to next slot with probability 1-p
quiz.explanation: It transmits with probability p and defers with q=1-p, repeating the check in the next slot.

clips.title: Where EX→EX and MEM→EX forwarding removes stalls
clips.hook: Trace a sub/and/or dependency to see exactly which pipeline stages must forward to avoid bubbles.
clips.summary: A sub producing R2 in cycle 3 can feed a dependent AND's ALU in cycle 4 via EX→EX forwarding, and the OR via MEM→EX forwarding. Later instructions read R2 from the register file since write-back has occurred by cycle 5, so no stalls are needed.

quiz.question: In the sub R2 / and R2 / or R2 / add R2 sequence, why do the AND and OR need forwarding but a later ADD does not?
options: The AND and OR read R2 before it is written to the register file, while the ADD reads it after write-back
Forwarding works only for two instructions
The ADD has a longer pipeline
The ADD uses a different ALU
quiz.explanation: The result is written to the register file in cycle 5, so only instructions reading in decode before then need forwarded values.

clips.title: Forwarding unit: muxes and register-compare control
clips.hook: How ALU input muxes and destination/source register comparisons select forwarded data.
clips.summary: Forwarding adds muxes at the ALU inputs choosing between register file output and results from the EX/MEM and MEM/WB pipeline registers. Control logic compares the source registers of the instruction in EX with destination registers of instructions in MEM and WB. The MEM-stage data is forwarded from the pipeline register preceding WB.

quiz.question: What does the forwarding control logic compare to decide whether to bypass the register file?
options: Program counter values
Cache tags
Source registers of the instruction in EX with destination registers in later pipeline stages
Opcodes of consecutive instructions
quiz.explanation: A match between EX's source registers and the MEM/WB destination registers triggers selecting the forwarded input.

clips.title: Load-use hazard: why forwarding can't remove the stall
clips.hook: Even with MEM→EX forwarding, a load followed by a dependent use needs a one-cycle delay.
clips.summary: Load data is available only at the end of the MEM stage, but a dependent instruction needs it at the start of its EX stage in the same cycle, so forwarding cannot help. One bubble is required, after which MEM→EX forwarding works. A compiler can fill the slot with an independent instruction instead of a no-op.

quiz.question: Why does an instruction immediately after a load that uses its result still need one stall despite forwarding?
options: Loads write back twice
Forwarding paths only exist from EX
The register file is too slow
Load data exists only after MEM, which is after the dependent instruction's EX would begin
quiz.explanation: Data arrives at the end of the load's MEM cycle, the same cycle the dependent needs it at EX start, so a one-cycle delay is needed.

clips.title: Shadowing vs Overriding: Static vs Dynamic Dispatch
clips.hook: How the parent's virtual declaration alone decides early vs late binding of a call through Shape*.
clips.summary: A virtual declaration in the base makes all matching child methods overrides, implicitly virtual. Calls resolve at runtime on the dynamic type. Without virtual, a redeclared method shadows and is bound at compile time on the static type. Call-site code alone cannot tell which happens; only the base declaration decides.

quiz.question: Shape* p points to a Triangle, and p->draw() is called. Triangle declares draw() with the same signature as Shape::draw. Which statement is correct?
options: Triangle::draw is called only if Triangle repeats the virtual keyword
Triangle::draw is always called because the dynamic type is Triangle
The call is undefined behavior if draw is not virtual
Shape::draw is called if Shape::draw is non-virtual, since binding uses the static type
quiz.explanation: Without virtual in the base, Triangle::draw merely shadows it and the call is bound statically to Shape::draw. This is well-defined. If the base is virtual, Triangle::draw overrides it, and repeating virtual is unnecessary.

clips.title: Virtual Destructors and Why Constructors Can't Be Virtual
clips.hook: Shadowed methods, delete through base pointer, and why a late-bound constructor makes no sense.
clips.summary: A virtual on a child method whose base is non-virtual does nothing, so the base version is called. delete invokes the destructor and then frees memory. Constructors cannot be virtual because construction needs the exact type at compile time. Destructors can be virtual, and then are resolved at runtime and chain through the parents.

quiz.question: Why can't a constructor be virtual in C++?
options: Constructing an object requires its exact dynamic type at compile time, and there is no object yet to dispatch on
Virtual functions can't be called on heap objects
Constructors have no this pointer
The vtable is stored in the destructor
quiz.explanation: Late binding dispatches on an existing object's dynamic type. During construction there is no such object, and the compiler must know the exact type to allocate and initialize it.

clips.title: Deleting Through a Base Pointer Needs a Virtual Destructor
clips.hook: What goes wrong when deleting a derived object via base pointer with a non-virtual destructor.
clips.summary: If a derived object is deleted through a base pointer and the base destructor is non-virtual, this is undefined behavior. The derived destructor is skipped, so members leak or locks stay held, and the wrong size may be freed, which can corrupt the heap. Marking only the derived destructor virtual does not help. The base destructor must be virtual.

quiz.question: Fruit has a non-virtual destructor, and Apple derives from Fruit with a virtual ~Apple(). What happens on `Fruit* f = new Apple; delete f;`?
options: Well-defined: only ~Fruit runs
A compile error
Undefined behavior, because ~Apple's virtual does not affect a call resolved through Fruit
Apple's destructor runs, then Fruit's
quiz.explanation: Virtual must be on the base destructor for dispatch through Fruit*. Otherwise deleting a derived object via a base pointer is UB, with possible leaks and wrong-size deallocation.

clips.title: Why full-batch GD costs 2.3 trillion terms
clips.hook: Count the per-step cost of gradient descent and see how SGD cuts it by a factor of N.
clips.summary: Full-batch gradient descent needs a term per sample per parameter per step: 23,000 parameters × 1M samples = 23 billion terms per step, over 2.3 trillion for 1,000 steps. SGD picks one random sample per step, cutting per-step cost by a factor of N.

quiz.question: Logistic regression has 23,000 parameters and 1M samples. About how many derivative terms does one full-batch GD step compute, and how does SGD with one sample change this?
options: 23 million; reduced by 23,000
2.3 trillion; reduced by 1,000
23 billion; reduced by a factor of 1 million
1 million; reduced by 1,000
quiz.explanation: Each of the 23,000 derivatives sums over 1M samples, giving 23 billion terms per step. One sample per step cuts that by 1M.

clips.title: Mini-batches and online updates in SGD
clips.hook: Mini-batches trade variance against cost, and SGD can absorb new data without restarting.
clips.summary: Strict SGD uses one sample per step, but mini-batches are more common. They give more stable parameter estimates in fewer steps than a single sample, and are much cheaper than full batch. Because SGD only needs the current parameters, new data can be used for one more step from the latest estimate without retraining from scratch.

quiz.question: Why can SGD incorporate newly arrived data without restarting from the initial parameters?
options: It stores all previous gradients and replays them
Each update depends only on the current parameters and the sample, so it can continue from the latest estimate
The learning rate is reset to zero after each sample
It always converges to the exact least-squares solution
quiz.explanation: The update rule is a function of the current parameters and a sample (or mini-batch), so one more step can be taken from the latest estimate.

clips.title: Star Schema: Fact vs Dimension Tables
clips.hook: How OLAP schemas separate append-only facts from stable dimensions via foreign keys.
clips.summary: A star schema has a large, often append-only fact table whose foreign keys (dimension attributes) reference smaller, stable dimension tables. Remaining dependent attributes such as quantity and price are the values queries aggregate.

quiz.question: In a star schema sales(storeID, itemID, custID, qty, price), which attributes are the typical targets of aggregation?
options: The dependent attributes qty and price
The foreign keys of the dimension tables
The dimension attributes storeID, itemID, custID
Only the primary keys of dimension tables
quiz.explanation: Dimension attributes are foreign keys used for joining and grouping. Dependent attributes (qty, price) are what get aggregated.

clips.title: Forwarding removes RAW stalls: temporal view
clips.hook: See how a bypass keeps CPI at 1 for back-to-back dependent ALU instructions.
clips.summary: Without bypassing, a dependent instruction must wait for the register write in cycle 5. With the EX output forwarded to the next instruction's EX input, no bubble is inserted and the pipeline keeps its rate. Similar forwarding from MEM output serves a dependent store.

clips.title: Load-use hazard: why bypassing can't save you
clips.hook: A load's data appears at the end of MEM, too late for the next instruction's EX.
clips.summary: For a load followed by a dependent instruction, the data is available only at the end of cycle 4 (MEM), but the consumer needs it at the start of its EX in cycle 3. Forwarding cannot go backward in time, so a stall is still required.

quiz.question: In a classic 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding, why does a load followed immediately by a dependent ALU instruction still need a stall?
options: The ALU cannot accept forwarded values from memory
The register file has only one read port
The loaded data is available only after MEM, later than the consumer's EX needs it
Forwarding paths only exist from the WB stage
quiz.explanation: Load data is produced at the end of MEM, but the consumer needs it at the start of its EX, which occurs one cycle earlier unless a bubble is inserted.

clips.title: Jumps vs. conditional branches: when is the target known?
clips.hook: Why branches cost more than jumps, and the idea of moving comparison into decode.
clips.summary: Jump targets are known after decode, from the immediate field, but conditional branches need the ALU comparison in EX to know whether they are taken. This motivates adding an ALU in decode to save a bubble.

quiz.question: Why does a conditional branch typically incur a larger penalty than an unconditional jump in this pipeline?
options: Jumps are always predicted correctly by the compiler
The branch condition is evaluated in EX, so taken-ness is unknown until then, whereas a jump target is known after decode
Jumps use a faster ALU
Conditional branches need memory access
quiz.explanation: Jump targets come from the immediate at decode, but conditional branches depend on the comparison in the ALU stage.

clips.title: Why downcasting needs a runtime check
clips.hook: Upcasts are implicit; downcasts from Entity* can't be verified statically, so dynamic_cast returns null on failure.
clips.summary: An upcast from Player to Entity is implicit, but a downcast from Entity* is unsafe since the dynamic type could be Player, Enemy or Entity. dynamic_cast checks the dynamic type at runtime and returns nullptr when the cast is invalid.

quiz.question: Given Entity* e that actually points to an Enemy, what does dynamic_cast<Player*>(e) yield?
options: nullptr
A compile-time error
A valid Player* with garbage members
An access violation always
quiz.explanation: For pointer casts, dynamic_cast checks the dynamic type at runtime and returns nullptr when the object is not a Player.
